why: The same query with the `?` dropped, so a failure says which half moved. An absent property never satisfies an operator — including `!=`, and that is the standing rule rather than an oversight, because three-valued logic everywhere would make `!=` mean two things depending on the corpus. So `ended>1893` excludes both rows that never ended, and only `spanning` survives. `>?` is the one place a caller opts out, one predicate at a time and where a reader can see it. A server that treats absence as satisfying an ordering answers 3 here and cannot be told apart from a conforming one by the case above.
